paras: The lynching of J. H. Howe took place at Fort Collins, Colorado, on the night of April 4, 1888, when a mob took Howe from the county jail and hanged him from a builders' derrick, hours after his arrest for killing his wife. Wire reports carried the story nationally, and a Denver Republican correspondent reported that doctors, lawyers and clergymen attended and that the town approved.

Howe, said to be about forty, had come to Fort Collins from Fredonia, New York, about 1880 with his wife, and the couple had a daughter of about six. Most reports called him a millwright, and descriptions of him ranged from "a prominent citizen" to "a worthless character." Several accounts described heavy drinking and abuse of his wife, who was said to support herself and their daughter by sewing.
According to one despatch, when Howe tried to beat her on Tuesday night, neighbors called Deputy Sheriff Stultz, but Mrs. Howe declined to have him locked up.

Around noon on Wednesday, April 4, Howe came home and found his wife packing to leave him after consulting Attorney Love about a divorce. He was accused of cutting her face and throat with a pocket-knife; she died within minutes at the gate. Sheriff Thomas R. Davy found Howe lying on a bed and took him to the county jail without resistance.

Through the afternoon men gathered at the jail, "fully a thousand" by the Denver Republican's count, and lynching was openly discussed while the sheriff kept a posse on guard. Its correspondent later wrote that citizens met that evening on Linden street to plan the lynching. Shortly after 8 o'clock the electric lights were cut as a signal.

The first-day special said 300 mounted men, some masked, knocked down Sheriff Davy, overpowered a posse of twenty and battered in the jail and cell doors. Howe, crying for mercy, was carried to a derrick at the new court house. He asked once more for his life, and the crowd answered with derision as some fifty men hauled on the rope. His body was cut down and taken to the hose house, where crowds came to view it the next day.

The Republican's correspondent reported "a feeling of relief" in Fort Collins and doubted that any prosecution could succeed. No report of an inquest or of arrests of mob members appears in the coverage. At year's end a list of "Victims of Judge Lynch" entered the case under April 4 as "J. Howe at Fort Collins, Colo."

The first wire, run in Washington's Evening Star as "A Wife Murderer Lynched," named the victim "Tom Howe," a laborer on "a protracted spree." A second wire, in the St. Paul Daily Globe and Rock Island Argus, called Howe "a prominent citizen."

Longer Denver Republican specials reached Wyoming papers a week later as "A Fort Collins Tragedy" and "Rope Justice," and the Indianapolis Journal ran the follow-up on April 17 as "A High-Toned Lynching Bee." These accounts called Howe a "wretch" with "cowardly cries," and the follow-up said the "outraged people took justice into their own hands." Headlines such as "Quick Justice" in the Huntsville Gazette and the Iowa Plain Dealer likewise presented the hanging as swift punishment.

A letter from Rev. E. G. Harbert of Fort Collins in the Parkersburg Freeman, "A High License Argument," instead blamed the town's high-license saloons for the "double tragedy." When the Presbyterian pastor told the mob to hang the saloon-keepers instead, Harbert wrote, some answered, "Better hang the preachers, and let the Saloon keepers alone." None of the reports states the race of Howe or his wife.

Accounts of the mob's size range from 300 men in the wire and first-day special and "several hundred" in one dispatch to about 500 in Harbert's letter and 1,000 in a brief. The Republican's follow-up put the storming party at about thirty, with three or four pinning the sheriff, whom other versions had knocked down or "put under guard." The first wire placed the murder on "Monday evening" and one brief on Thursday, but the Fort Collins accounts and Harbert's letter agree on Wednesday, April 4.

bases: A mob took Howe, accused of murdering his wife, from the county jail and hanged him (A10, A6, A14).

Every account has Howe hanged by a mob numbering from about thirty to hundreds after it overpowered the sheriff (A10, A6, A14); the papers framed it as punishment for his wife's murder, the 'unwritten warrant' of 'outraged people' (A6).
Independent wires and specials (A1, A2, A7, A10) and a letter from a Fort Collins resident (A14) agree that a mob took Howe from jail and hanged him on April 4.

framing.detail: Short wires headed 'A Wife Murderer Lynched', 'He Was Lynched' and 'A Corpse for a Football' told the murder and the hanging without comment.
The Denver Republican correspondent wrote that 'outraged people took justice into their own hands' and reported general approval, reprinted as 'A High-Toned Lynching Bee'.
Heads 'Quick Justice' and 'Rope Justice' and the specials' language ('wretch', 'cowardly cries', 'worthless body') presented the hanging as deserved punishment.
The Freeman printed a minister's letter, 'A High License Argument', that called the mob 'infuriated' and lawless but aimed its blame at the saloons.
